title: Resulting String After Adjacent Removals
statement:
You are given a string `s` of lowercase English letters. Call two letters *neighbours* when they sit next to each other in the alphabet, in either order; the alphabet wraps around, so `'a'` and `'z'` are neighbours as well.

As long as `s` has two adjacent characters that are neighbours, delete the leftmost such adjacent pair and close the gap. Return the string that remains once no such pair is left (it may be empty).
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Following the rule literally (find the leftmost removable pair, cut it out, search again) costs O(n²) or worse. Notice what is left of a prefix once it has been fully reduced: it contains no removable pair. So a new character can only pair with the last surviving character, and if it does, that pair is the leftmost one available, because nothing further left can be removed and nothing further right has been read yet. That is exactly a stack.

## Approach

1. Keep `stack`, the characters that survive so far, in order.
2. For each character `ch` of `s`, if the stack is not empty, compute `gap`, the distance between the character codes of the top and `ch`.
3. A `gap` of 1 means alphabet neighbours, and 25 means the `a`/`z` wrap. In either case pop the top: the pair disappears and `ch` is never pushed.
4. Otherwise push `ch`.
5. Join the stack into the answer.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abc"`.

- `a`: the stack is empty, so push it: `[a]`.
- `b`: the top is `a` and `gap = 1`, so pop: `[]`.
- `c`: the stack is empty again, so push it: `[c]`.

Joining gives `"c"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each character is pushed at most once and popped at most once.
- Space: O(n) for the stack.

## Pitfalls

- The alphabet wraps: `a` and `z` are neighbours (their codes differ by 25), so `"zadb"` becomes `"db"`.
- Equal letters are not neighbours: `"aa"` stays as it is.
- The order of removals matters. In `"cba"` the leftmost pair `cb` goes first and `"a"` remains; removing `ba` first would wrongly leave `"c"`. Reading left to right with a stack respects this automatically.
- After a pop, the new top may pair with the next character: in `"adcb"`, removing `dc` exposes `a`, which then pairs with `b`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack` | the surviving characters so far, bottom to top in string order |
| `ch` | the character being read |
| `gap` | the absolute difference between the codes of the top and `ch` |

narration.2: stack holds the characters that survive so far; no two adjacent ones in it form a removable pair.
narration.3: Read the string from left to right.
narration.4: Only a non-empty stack has a top that ch could pair with.
narration.5: Measure how far apart the top and ch are in the alphabet.
narration.6: A gap of 1 means alphabet neighbours, and 25 is the wrap between a and z.
narration.7: Remove the pair: drop the top, and ch is never added.
narration.8: Move on to the next character.
narration.11: No pair formed, so ch survives for now.
narration.13: The stack, read from bottom to top, is the final string.
